name: Gerald Ford
role: Presided over the Fall of Saigon. Not one of the four who managed the war; the one who managed its ending: asked Congress for the aid Nixon had promised in private, was refused, and ordered the evacuation.

numbers.k: US troops in Vietnam on arrival
numbers.v: about 50, the Defense Attaché Office and the embassy Marines
about 7,000 in 19 hours by helicopter; about 130,000 Vietnamese by sea and air in April overall

decisions: Sworn in. Writes to Thieu the next day that the commitments of his predecessor still stand; they do not, because Congress holds them.
Phuoc Long province falls, the first whole province lost since 1973. No US response; Hanoi reads it as the test it was.
Asks Congress for $300 million more for Saigon; hearings, no vote.
Sends Weyand to Saigon to assess. Weyand reports on 4 April: it can hold with $722 million and air support; Ford knows the second is illegal and the first is unlikely.
Operation Babylift ordered; the first C-5A crashes the next day, 138 dead.
Address to Congress asking for the $722 million; several members walk out.
Tulane: the war is “finished as far as America is concerned”. The line is applauded; Kissinger was not told it was in the speech.
Approves Frequent Wind in principle; Ambassador Martin still resists.
Orders the evacuation at 1048 Saigon time after the rocket attack on Tan Son Nhut kills the last two Marines.
Saigon falls at 1130 local. Ford’s statement: the evacuation is complete; it “closes a chapter”.
The Mayaguez, seized by the Khmer Rouge: 41 Americans die retaking a ship whose crew had already been released. The last names on the Wall.
days: Ban Me Thuot attacked before dawn by three PAVN divisions; falls in two days.
Thieu tells his generals the Highlands may have to be given up; Ban Me Thuot lost.
Thieu decides at Cam Ranh to withdraw from Pleiku and Kontum down Route 7B, an abandoned road.
The order given; General Phu leaves by helicopter before his troops.
The Route 7B column of 200,000 soldiers and civilians is caught at the Ba River. The convoy of tears.
Quang Tri abandoned. In Washington, Ford’s aid request is still in committee.
Thieu reverses the order to hold Hue: hold it. Then reverses again.
Route 1 cut south of Hue; the city is isolated.
Tam Ky and Quang Ngai fall; the coast is a line of retreats.
Hue falls. Ford sends Weyand.
Chu Lai evacuated by sea.
Weyand arrives in Saigon; the Da Nang airlift begins with 727s landing under fire.
Panic at Da Nang; the last World Airways flight leaves with soldiers on the wheel wells.
Da Nang falls. A hundred thousand ARVN gone as an army in a week. The gauge now reads about 24 provinces of 44.
Hanoi’s Politburo moves the target from 1976 to April 1975: the Ho Chi Minh Campaign.
Qui Nhon and Nha Trang fall; Thieu’s cabinet resigns.
Tuy Hoa; Weyand’s draft report says the situation is critical and the odds long.
Cam Ranh; Ford orders Babylift; refugee ships pulling into Vung Tau with the dead on deck.
The C-5A crashes on take-off from Tan Son Nhut, 138 dead, 78 of them children. Weyand reports to Ford at Palm Springs.
A South Vietnamese pilot bombs the presidential palace and flies north.
Xuan Loc: the PAVN 4th Corps attacks; the 18th Division holds. The one stand.
Ford’s address to Congress; the request is not taken up.
Operation Eagle Pull: the US embassy in Phnom Penh evacuated by helicopter. Sirik Matak declines the seat: he will die where he is, and does.
Ford reads a State Department cable predicting Saigon can hold a month; the CIA says less.
Phnom Penh falls to the Khmer Rouge. The dominoes fall in the wrong order.
Ford orders the evacuation of all non-essential Americans; Martin slows it, fearing panic.
Xuan Loc abandoned after twelve days; the road to Saigon open. Martin tells Thieu it is time to go.
Thieu resigns on television, blaming the Americans, in a speech of ninety minutes. Xuan Loc falls.
Ford at Tulane: finished. The Senate Armed Services Committee stops hearing the aid request.
Thieu flies to Taiwan on a CIA aircraft with what he can carry.
The PAVN begins the final assault from five directions; 130,000 troops against the city.
Rockets hit Saigon for the first time since 1973; Bien Hoa air base under fire.
Duong Van Minh — “Big Minh”, who overthrew Diem in 1963 — sworn in as president to negotiate; Tan Son Nhut bombed by captured A-37s flown by defectors.

Rockets at 0358 kill Corporal McMahon and Lance Corporal Judge at the DAO gate. Fixed-wing evacuation ends; Ford orders Frequent Wind at 1048; “White Christmas” on the radio; 81 helicopters, 19 hours.

Martin leaves the roof at 0458; the last eleven Marines at 0753. T-54 tank 843 through the palace gate at 1130; Minh surrenders; the city is Ho Chi Minh City by the afternoon. Ford’s statement, 1330 Washington time.
Ford asks Congress for $507 million for refugees; it passes on 21 May. The lead-up is over and the after begins in the section below.

lives.title: A Rumor of War
lives.note: A Marine lieutenant in the first landing at Da Nang, 1965; the first of the memoirs to say plainly what the war did to the men who fought it.

lives.title: Dispatches
lives.note: Esquire’s correspondent; the book that gave the war its prose style and Apocalypse Now its narration.

lives.title: Born on the Fourth of July
lives.note: Paralysed at twenty-one; the wheelchair at the 1972 Republican convention; the film in 1989.

lives.title: The Things They Carried
lives.note: Drafted in 1968, considered Canada, went. Fiction that says at the start it is fiction, so that the true parts can be told.

lives.title: Going After Cacciato
lives.note: A soldier walks to Paris. National Book Award.

lives.title: Matterhorn
lives.note: Thirty years in the writing by a Marine lieutenant with the Navy Cross; the war as work.

lives.title: The Sorrow of War
lives.note: From the other side: a PAVN veteran, one of ten survivors of a brigade of five hundred; banned in Vietnam for years.

lives.title: The Sympathizer
lives.note: Opens with the fall of Saigon from inside the evacuation; the Pulitzer.

lives.title: A Bright Shining Lie
lives.note: John Paul Vann and the whole war through one adviser’s life; sixteen years to write.

lives.title: The Best and the Brightest
lives.note: How the advisers of projects 40–43 got it wrong, written while they were still in office.

lives.title: Dien Cai Dau
lives.note: A Black soldier’s poems; “Facing It”, at the Wall, is the one everyone reads.

lives.title: Vietnam Veterans Memorial
lives.note: A black granite wall sunk into the Mall with 58,000 names in order of death and no figures. Chosen at twenty-one from 1,421 entries; fought over; then the most visited memorial in Washington. The names are still being added.

lives.title: The Three Soldiers
lives.note: The figurative statue added by compromise, facing the Wall. This repository does not draw faces; the statue does.

lives.title: Vietnam Women’s Memorial
lives.note: The 265,000 women who served, 11,000 in country.

lives.title: The Napalm Girl
lives.note: Phan Thi Kim Phuc, aged nine, on Route 1 at Trang Bang; the Pulitzer; she lives in Canada.

lives.title: Saigon Execution
lives.note: General Loan, the second day of Tet. Adams said the photograph killed the general and that two people died in it.

lives.title: The Deer Hunter
lives.note: The steel town and the Russian roulette that did not happen; Best Picture.

lives.title: Apocalypse Now
lives.note: Conrad up the river; the film that took the war into myth, and the making of it nearly killed its makers.

lives.title: Platoon
lives.note: By a veteran of the 25th Infantry; Best Picture; the first the veterans said was theirs.

lives.title: Full Metal Jacket
lives.note: Parris Island and Hue, shot in London.

lives.title: Hearts and Minds
lives.note: The documentary; Westmoreland on the value of life in the Orient, cut against a funeral. Best Documentary while the war was still on.

lives.title: The Fog of War
lives.note: McNamara at eighty-five, eleven lessons, still counting.

lives.title: The Vietnam War
lives.note: Eighteen hours; Vietnamese voices from both sides for the first time on American television.

lives.title: “Fortunate Son”
lives.note: Who got drafted and who did not, in two minutes twenty.

lives.title: “What’s Going On”
lives.note: Written after his brother came home from Vietnam and told him.

lives.title: Post-traumatic stress disorder
lives.note: Named after the veterans’ rap groups and Shatan and Lifton’s work made the case; about 15% of male theatre veterans had it in 1988 and about 30% had had it at some point. It is what the user means by a lifelong conflict.

lives.title: Agent Orange
lives.note: Nineteen million gallons; the VA presumes fourteen conditions service-connected; the Vietnamese count some three million affected and the children of the sprayed. The lawsuit settled in 1984 for $180 million.

lives.title: The boat people
lives.note: The after for the other side; the Orderly Departure Program from 1979; 1.6 million Vietnamese Americans by 2010.

lives.title: The MIA flag
lives.note: 1,587 still unaccounted for in 2020; the only flag besides the Stars and Stripes to fly over the White House by statute. Some men never came home because they were never found; some never came home because they did.

advisers.post: Secretary of State and National Security Adviser
advisers.note: Argued for the aid to the end; argued against the Tulane line; drafted the “chapter” statement.
Wanted the evacuation earlier and faster; fired in November.

advisers.post: Army Chief of Staff; the April mission

advisers.note: Kept the tamarind tree in the embassy courtyard standing until the afternoon of the 29th so as not to signal panic; it was cut down for the helicopters.
Ran the evacuation from the Situation Room.
The station’s estimates were the accurate ones and were not the ones Martin used.
Sent the last cable: “it has been a long fight and we have lost.”
Flew out the ARVN’s aircraft and ships so they would not be captured; the last quartermaster.

text: Ford: the lead-up to the Fall of Saigon a day at a time from Ban Me Thuot to the palace gate, and the lives after it — the books, the art, the films, the diagnoses — because for a lot of men the conflict did not end on 30 April 1975.
